result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), describing them as devastating neurological disorders affecting 4 in 10,000 infants per year, characterized by recurrent seizures, developmental delay, and drug resistance. DEEs are commonly caused by mutations in ion channels, particularly sodium channelopathies, with variants in SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, and auxiliary subunits including FGF12 and FGF13 being implicated.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C13-C28) represent well-established background knowledge supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The epidemiological data, clinical characteristics, and genetic causes are appropriately referenced and provide necessary context for the study.

result: The manuscript establishes that FGF13 variants are implicated in DEEs, but the mechanisms are unclear because FGF13 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, undergoes extensive alternative splicing producing multiple isoforms with distinct functions, and has incompletely cataloged roles. Prior work suggested conflicting mechanisms: gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons versus loss-of-function in inhibitory neurons. Excitatory neurons predominantly express Fgf13-S while inhibitory neurons express both Fgf13-S and Fgf13-VY.
evaluation: These claims (C3-C5, C29-C47) accurately summarize prior knowledge and identify gaps in understanding that motivate the current study. The claims are well-supported by citations to relevant literature and establish the rationale for the cell-type-specific knockout approach.

result: Whole-brain neuronal knockout of Fgf13 using Nestin-Cre resulted in near-complete absence of FGF13 in hippocampus, perinatal mortality with median survival of 17 days, spontaneous seizures starting at P12, developmental delay (smaller body size), and susceptibility to hyperthermia-induced seizures. Heterozygous females showed reduced survival (60% past 1 month), suggesting a gene dosage effect.
evaluation: Claims C48-C58 are well-supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including western blots (Figure 1B), immunohistochemistry (Figure 1C), survival curves (Figure 1D), body mass measurements (Figure 1E), video documentation (Video 1), and hyperthermia seizure assays (Figure 1F). The gene dosage interpretation is reasonable based on comparing hemizygous males to heterozygous females.

result: Excitatory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 using Emx1-Cre resulted in loss of FGF13-S and FGF13-U isoforms while preserving FGF13-VY and FGF13-V. These mice were born at expected ratios, survived to adulthood, showed no differences in body size, and exhibited no seizures during hyperthermia protocol or by EEG. Emx1-Fgf13 cKO neurons showed diminished long-term inactivation of sodium channels, but this deficit was not sufficient to cause seizures.
evaluation: Claims C59-C70 are strongly supported by western blots (Figure 2A), immunohistochemistry (Figure 2B), survival data (Figure 2C), body mass measurements (Figure 2D), seizure assays (Figure 2E), EEG recordings (Figure 2F), and electrophysiological measurements (Figure 2G). The conclusion that loss of Fgf13 from excitatory neurons is insufficient for seizures is well-justified by the absence of seizure phenotypes despite demonstrable loss of long-term inactivation.

result: Inhibitory neuron-targeted deletion of Fgf13 using Gad2-Cre eliminated FGF13 from one-third of GFP+ interneurons, with preferential loss of FGF13-VY and FGF13-Y isoforms. Male Gad2-Fgf13 cKO mice showed complete perinatal lethality (median survival 14.5 days), smaller body and brain size, and universal susceptibility to hyperthermia-induced seizures. Heterozygous females showed reduced but less severe survival deficits, suggesting gene dosage effects. Interneuron numbers were not reduced, indicating the phenotype results from functional deficits rather than cell loss.
evaluation: Claims C71-C86 are comprehensively supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 3A-B), western blots (Figure 3C), survival curves (Figure 3D), body/brain mass measurements (Figure 3E), seizure assays (Figure 3F-G), and cell counting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). The conclusion that FGF13 deficiency in inhibitory neurons is the major contributor to seizures is well-justified by comparing phenotypes across different knockout models.

result: Unbiased metabolomic analysis of Gad2-Fgf13 cKO brains revealed marked differences from wildtype, with features consistent with severe seizures. L-kynurenine was the most enriched metabolite (Log2FC=2.58, p=0.0009), glycolysis was the most enriched KEGG pathway among upregulated metabolites (p=4.29E-6), and methionine metabolism was the most downregulated pathway (p=9.88E-4), all consistent with seizure pathology in patients.
evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by metabolomic data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2) and appropriately compared to patient data through citations. The metabolomic changes provide independent validation of the severity of the seizure phenotype and strengthen the overall conclusions.

result: Re-analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data showed highest Fgf13 enrichment in axo-axonic and MGE neurogliaform/Ivy cells expressing Nkx2.1. Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice targeting MGE-derived interneurons showed intermediate phenotypes: ~40% survival past 1 month (median 22 days), smaller body size, and nearly universal susceptibility to hyperthermia-induced seizures. The reduced severity compared to Gad2-Fgf13 cKO suggests MGE-derived neurons are partially responsible for the phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C93-C103 are supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B), immunohistochemistry (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), survival data (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), body mass measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E), and seizure assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F). The interpretation that MGE-derived neurons are partially responsible is reasonable based on the intermediate phenotype severity, though the hypothesis nature of this conclusion (C103) is appropriately acknowledged.

result: Pyramidal cells in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO hippocampi showed increased frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) and decreased frequency of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) compared to wildtype, with no changes in amplitude. These frequency changes without amplitude changes indicate a presynaptic mechanism, suggesting that Fgf13 ablation in inhibitory neurons decreased inhibitory drive onto pyramidal cells, thereby increasing pyramidal cell excitability.
evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings from acute hippocampal slices (Figure 4A-D). The interpretation that frequency changes without amplitude changes indicate a presynaptic mechanism is standard in the field. The conclusion that reduced inhibitory drive increases pyramidal cell excitability logically follows from the data and provides a circuit-level mechanism for the seizure phenotype.

result: Cultured Gad2-Fgf13 cKO interneurons showed decreased intrinsic excitability with reduced spike numbers at higher current injections and increased susceptibility to depolarization block at lower current levels. Progressive changes in action potential parameters (reduced peak amplitude and dV/dt max, increased APD50, elevated interspike membrane voltage) in the second and third spikes suggest growing repolarization deficits. Surprisingly, NaV current amplitude and steady-state inactivation were unchanged, but K+ current density was significantly reduced.
evaluation: Claims C109-C120 are comprehensively supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 5A-I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The finding that NaV currents are unaffected while K+ currents are reduced is particularly important as it challenges the prevailing hypothesis that FGF13 primarily regulates NaV channels. The data quality appears robust with appropriate sample sizes and statistical analyses.

result: Viral re-expression of either Fgf13-VY or Fgf13-S in Gad2-Fgf13 cKO neurons partially rescued excitability deficits, with increased action potential firing at higher current injections and reduced probability of depolarization block, though neither isoform alone fully restored wildtype phenotypes. Fgf13-S specifically increased K+ current density to wildtype levels and partially hyperpolarized interspike membrane potential, suggesting FGF13-S increases repolarizing K+ currents. Both isoforms contribute to inhibitory interneuron function.
evaluation: Claims C121-C129 are supported by rescue experiments using AAV-mediated re-expression (Figure 6A-H). The partial rescue by individual isoforms is important evidence that both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY contribute to interneuron function. The specific rescue of K+ currents by FGF13-S provides mechanistic insight. However, the inability to test both isoforms simultaneously is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

result: The study resolves conflicting prior reports by demonstrating that Fgf13 ablation and loss of both FGF13-S and FGF13-VY in inhibitory interneurons reduces inhibitory drive onto hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Both isoforms are required for proper interneuron function, as re-expression of either alone only partially restored excitability. This provides a unifying explanation for reports suggesting either gain-of-function effects in excitatory neurons or loss-of-function in inhibitory neurons.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132, C139 represent the main integrative conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence from multiple knockout models, electrophysiological characterization, and rescue experiments. The resolution of conflicting prior reports is a significant contribution that advances understanding of FGF13-related DEE mechanisms.

result: The findings emphasize that alternative splicing is an important source of protein diversity in the mammalian brain. FGF13 has the most extensive set of alternatively spliced isoforms among FHFs and exhibits uniquely segregated splice variant expression patterns among distinct neuron cell types, with one of the highest differential isoform expression (DIE) values across neuronal cell types.
evaluation: Claims C133-C137 are supported by citations to prior literature and the authors' previous work on Fgf13 splice variant expression. These claims provide important context for interpreting the functional significance of the different isoforms and their cell-type-specific expression patterns.

result: The results are consistent with available patient data. The inability to completely rescue electrophysiological consequences with either FGF13-S or FGF13-VY alone suggests that other isoforms (e.g., FGF13-U, FGF13-V) may also make critical contributions.
evaluation: Claims C138 and C140 represent reasonable interpretations and acknowledgments of study limitations. The consistency with patient data strengthens the translational relevance, while the speculation about other isoforms is appropriately cautious and identifies directions for future research.

result: The data provide clear evidence that seizure susceptibility is attributable to Fgf13 knockout in inhibitory interneurons rather than excitatory neurons. Gene dosage effects are evident from reduced survival in heterozygous females compared to wildtype. Recurrent uncontrolled seizures are a major risk factor for sudden death, consistent with the observed SUDEP-like phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C141-C148 synthesize key findings and are well-supported by the comparative analysis across different knockout models. The gene dosage interpretation is strengthened by consistent observations across multiple genotypes. The connection to SUDEP is appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature.

result: Complete neuronal knockout with Nestin-Cre showed relatively increased survival compared to interneuron-specific knockout with Gad2-Cre. This could be due to less efficient targeting of interneurons by Nestin-Cre or may reflect biological compensation from simultaneous loss of excitation and inhibition. The observation that Emx1-Fgf13 cKO mice do not suffer seizures is consistent with an earlier study.
evaluation: Claims C149-C153 present observations and speculations about differences between knockout models. While the survival difference is documented (C149), the explanations (C150-C151) are explicitly speculative and not directly tested. The consistency with prior work (C152-C153) provides some support but doesn't resolve the mechanistic uncertainty. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between technical and biological explanations.

result: The study confirms that FGF13-S confers long-term inactivation and that ablation of Fgf13 in excitatory neurons eliminates long-term inactivation, yet this mechanism does not contribute to seizure susceptibility. Instead, knockout of Fgf13 in excitatory neurons appears to affect learning and memory rather than causing seizures.
evaluation: Claims C154-C158 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 2G) showing loss of long-term inactivation in Emx1-Fgf13 cKO neurons, combined with the absence of seizures in these mice. This challenges the prior hypothesis (C155) that reduced long-term inactivation drives seizures. The reference to learning and memory effects (C158) is appropriately cited to prior literature.

result: The knockout models cannot provide direct insight into how missense variants in patients contribute to seizures, but the Emx1-Fgf13 cKO model provides new boundaries on how missense variants act in excitatory neurons. Fgf13 ablation led to relatively minor effects on neuronal voltage-gated Na+ currents in excitatory neurons compared to previous results using different approaches. The knockout model likely represents a more relevant disease model than knockdown approaches or acute antibody infusion.
evaluation: Claims C159-C162 appropriately acknowledge limitations while highlighting strengths of the approach. The limitation regarding missense variants (C159) is important and honest. The comparison to prior studies (C161) and the argument for model relevance (C162) are reasonable, though the claim that knockout is more relevant than other approaches could be debated depending on the specific question being addressed.

result: Loss of FGF13 in inhibitory interneurons confers seizure susceptibility through a mechanism that surprisingly does not affect NaV currents. This fits with prior findings that NaV1.1 has reduced FHF binding, rendering NaV1.1 channels poor targets for FHF regulation. Instead, perturbed excitability results from reduced K+ currents, consistent with findings in cardiomyocytes. These data support growing recognition that FHFs exert effects beyond NaV channel regulation.
evaluation: Claims C163-C168 present a key mechanistic finding that challenges prevailing assumptions about FGF13 function. The lack of NaV current changes (C163) is well-documented experimentally. The connection to prior work on NaV1.1 (C164-C165) and cardiomyocytes (C167) strengthens the interpretation. The conclusion about FHF functions beyond NaV regulation (C168) is an important contribution to the field.

result: The mechanism by which FGF13 affects K+ currents is not known, as direct interaction between FHFs and K+ channels has not been detected. The identified role for FGF13 in stabilizing microtubules may contribute, as microtubules regulate trafficking of ion channels to the plasma membrane during channel biogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C169-C170 acknowledge a gap in mechanistic understanding and offer a speculative explanation. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by a citation about microtubule function in channel trafficking (C170), it remains untested in this study. The honest acknowledgment of what is not known (C169) is appropriate.

result: The data are consistent with a possible role for FGF13 in chandelier cell function. Chandelier cells are fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons that target the axon initial segment of pyramidal cells and are found sparsely but are highly branched. Fgf13 has been identified as important for chandelier cell axon development, and chandelier cells originate from the MGE. The Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO mice target these cells, suggesting FGF13 may regulate chandelier cell function in seizure generation. In the current model, decreased interneuron excitability results in a pro-excitatory state.
evaluation: Claims C171-C179 present a reasonable hypothesis about chandelier cell involvement supported by the Nkx2.1-Fgf13 cKO data and prior literature. While not directly tested (C171 acknowledges this), the inference is well-grounded in the experimental results and established knowledge about chandelier cells. The observation that decreased interneuron excitability leads to a pro-excitatory state (C179) is directly supported by the data.
